content: 864 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON POWER ELECTRONICS, VOL. 17, NO. 6, NOVEMBER 2002 Engineering Design of Lossless Passive Soft Switching Methods for PWM Converters—Part II. With Non-Minimum Voltage Stress Circuit Cells K. Mark Smith, Jr., Member, IEEE, and Keyue Ma Smedley, Senior Member, IEEE Abstract—This paper proposes the analysis and design methodology of lossless, passive soft switching methods for PWM converters. The emphasis of the design and analysis is for PWM converters that use nonminimum voltage stress (non-MVS) circuit cells to provide soft switching. PWM converters with non-MVS circuit cells have several distinct advantages over converters that use minimum voltage stress (MVS) cells. With the same relative size of the inductor and capacitor added for soft switching, the non-MVS cells have a substantially larger duty ratio range where soft switching is guaranteed. In addition, the over-current stress of the main switch, under most conditions, will be lower and an optimum value of inductor and capacitor added for soft switching can be used. Therefore, with proper design, the non-MVS cells provide higher efficiency. These advantages are obtained with the price of higher switching voltage stress and one additional inductor. The loss model for a MOSFET and optimum capacitor and inductor values are utilized in the design procedure. Examples of the design procedure are given for PFC and dc–dc applications. Experimental results backup the claim of higher efficiency. Index Terms—Lossless snubber, passive lossless softswitching, softswitching. I. INTRODUCTION P ASSIVE soft switching methods that add small inductors, capacitors, and diodes to a pulse width modulated (PWM) converter can provide soft turn-on and turn-off of the active switches if they are placed properly [1]. A capacitor is used to provide soft turn-off of the main switch, and an inductor is used to provide zero current turn-on. Besides properly placing the small inductor and capacitor, additional circuitry must be used to losslessly recover the energy collected in these devices. In [1] the authors describe a procedure to synthesize soft switching converters based on a set of properties and the use of the circuit cells shown in Table I. With proper placement of these cells into a converter, they will provide soft switching and recovery of the saved energy. The circuit cells are grouped into a set of min- imum voltage stress (MVS) circuit cells (cells I, II) and a set of nonminimum voltage stress (non-MVS) circuit cells (cells III, IV, V, VI). The non-MVS cells add additional voltage stress across the main switch, while the MVS cells do not. However, the non-MVS cells have several distinct advantages over the others. This paper proposes the analysis and design methodology of lossless passive soft switching converters that use non-MVS cir- cuit cells. The analysis of the cells is generalized so it can be applied to any PWM converter with the cell inserted. In addi- tion, operation of just the turn-on version of these cells is de- scribed to show how in certain applications the over-voltage stress on the main switch is independent of current. The design goal is to minimize switching losses while still maintaining soft switching over the desired operating range. The loss model for a MOSFET and optimum capacitor and inductor values derived in [3] are utilized in the design procedure. Examples of the de- sign procedure are given for power factor correcting (PFC) and DC–DC applications. Experimental efficiency results show that for a unity PFC application, the non-MVS cells obtain higher efficiency than the MVS cells. Section II includes the analysis of the non-MVS cells. Sec- tion III derives the optimum inductor and capacitor values. Sec- tion IV describes the design procedure. Section V shows experi- mental results and compares the non-MVS cells with MVS cells. Between the Conclusion and Reference list is the Appendix that contains the stage equations for the cells. II. EXPERIMENTAL RESULT AND COMPARISON An experimental efficiency comparison was made between different soft switching PFC boost converters using both non-MVS and MVS cells. The compared circuits included the PFC boost converter using non-MVS cell III designed in the last section [Fig. 1(a)] and a comparable PFC boost converter using a MVS cell (cell I) designed in [3]. In addition, two different boost converters using the turn-on only version of cell III (i.e., without and ). These converters, use the same inductors as designed for the compete cell III. If the design procedure was followed for these turn-on only versions, a larger inductors could be used. For this comparison, the original values were maintained to compare the turn-off losses with the complete non-MVS cells. Moreover, one circuit used the same gate driver (UC3710) as the complete non-MVS and MVS cells, and the other used a driver with a lower gate resistance (see [4, Fig. 2] with a ZTX749 PNP for turn-off). The results for static and dynamic PFC efficiency results are shown in Figs. 10 and 9. For the static PFC operation, DC–DC efficiency of the converter was taken so that the input voltage and current were identical to a particular operating point on the PFC line cycle (max load). The dynamic PFC tests operated the converter as a PFC at different power levels. The results show that the non-MVS cell achieved higher ef- ficiency than the MVS cell. This is because a and value can be selected closer to the optimum value. The soft switching range is higher, and the over-current stress is lower. When and Ds1 are removed from Cell III to provide only soft turn-on, the efficiency dropped as expected. However, if a faster gate driver is used, then the efficiency can be increased higher than the compete non-MVS cell. The hard turn-off circuit has higher turn-off losses in the active switch as expected, increasing its heat sink, but the overall losses are smaller because of less cir- culating energy. Table III summarizes the comparison between the non-MVS cells and MVS cells [5], [6]. VI. CONCLUSION The non-MVS cells have shown excellent efficiency for a PFC boost converter. As compared to the MVS cells they give higher efficiency but add voltage stress to the active switch and need one extra inductor. For applications where this stress can be tolerated and optimum efficiency is needed, then the non-MVS cells show excellent promise. When minimizing overall losses is more important than minimizing active switch losses and cost, then the hard turn-off version of the non-MVS cells coupled with a more expensive faster gate driver shows the best results. The design procedure minimized switching losses while en- suring that soft switching was maintained over the desired op- erating range. This was accomplished by limiting the resonant period of and to some portion of the switching period and then using this constraint to find optimized values for and . The analysis was presented in a general format so that the equations are valid for any converter the cell may be placed into.

Mark Smith, Jr. (M’93) received the B.S. degree in electrical and computer engineering from the Uni- versity of Colorado, Boulder, in 1990 and the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in electrical engineering from the University of California, Irvine, in 1995 and 1999 re- spectively. Since 1999, he has been working in industry de- signing high power converters and amplifiers. He has published more than 12 conference and journal pa- pers in the area of power electronics. His research interests include soft switching of power converters, and precision analog and digital control of switching power amplifiers. He has been awarded one U.S. patent in the area of power electronics. Keyue Ma Smedley (SM’97) received the B.S. and M.S. degrees in electrical engineering from Zhejiang University, China, in 1982 and 1985, respectively, and the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in electrical engi- neering from the California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, in 1987 and 1991, respectively. She was an Engineer at the Superconducting Super Collider, from 1990 to 1992, where she was respon- sible for the design and specification of ac–dc conver- sion systems for all accelerator rings. She joined the faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Uni- versity of California, Irvine, in 1992, where she has established a state-of-the-art Power Electronics Laboratory. Her research interest includes control, topolo- gies, and integration of dc–dc converters, high fidelity class-D power ampli- fiers, active and passive soft switching techniques, single-phase and three-phase power factor corrected rectifiers, active power filters, and grid-connected in- verters for alternative energy sources, etc. Dr. Smedley is an At-Large AdCom member of the IEEE Power Electronics Society, the Chair of IEEE Power Electronics Society Constitution and Bylaws Committee, an Associate Editor of IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON POWER ELECTRONICS, a faculty member of Eta Kappa Nu, a Co-Chair of Industry/Ed- ucation Committee of the Power Sources Manufacturer’s Association, and the Chair of IASTED and IEEE Power Electronics Society cosponsored International Symposium on Power Generation and Renewable Energy Sources 2002.
